{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_014UCxkkMTj6y1zApWKC6gjQ","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# BUILD PLAN — output format\n2\t\n3\tEmit the plan in exactly these sections, in this order. Keep it concrete: name real\n4\ttechnologies and real checks, not placeholders. Length is not quality: prefer one-line table\n5\tcells, cite IDs (V2, Phase 3, E1) instead of restating content, and scale the plan to the system.\n6\tA section with nothing load-bearing is one line (\"None.\", \"N/A — <reason>\"); a section that a\n7\tdeclared exception makes moot is one line citing it.\n8\t\n9\t---\n10\t\n11\t## 1. Classification and constraints\n12\t- **What:** one line on the system.\n13\t- **Type:** software / infra / AI-agentic (or a mix); greenfield or brownfield; small build or not.\n14\t- **Dominant constraint:** correctness | availability | latency | cost | scale | compliance.\n15\t- **Worst failure:** the single failure that would hurt most.\n16\t\n17\t**Budgets** (only the rows that bind; add rows the system needs, such as a cutover freeze window):\n18\t\n19\t| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n20\t|---|---|---|---|\n21\t| Latency | … | REQUIREMENT / BASELINE / ASSUMPTION / UNKNOWN | V… or Phase … |\n22\t| Throughput | … | … | … |\n23\t| Availability / SLO | … | … | … |\n24\t| RPO / RTO | … | … | … |\n25\t| Resource use | … | … | … |\n26\t| AI inference cost | … (AI systems only) | … | … |\n27\t| Storage cost | … | … | … |\n28\t| Operational complexity | … (e.g. services to run, on-call load) | … | … |\n29\t\n30\tAn UNKNOWN target has no number: write the missing input, who supplies it, and the phase that\n31\tneeds it. An ASSUMPTION gives its basis.\n32\t\n33\t**Missing inputs:** the unknowns that would change the plan most, and any assumption the phase\n34\torder rests on.\n35\t\n36\t## 2. Dependency map\n37\tOnly the dependencies that bind and that the phase order does not already show:\n38\t\n39\t| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n40\t|---|---|---|---|\n41\t| … | … | decision / validation / risk-security / organizational / economic (structural or runtime only when surprising) | built / deployed / specified / hardened / exposed / committed |\n42\t\n43\tThen one line naming the kinds with no instance (\"No organizational or economic dependencies.\").\n44\tIn brownfield work, mark each dependency CONFIRMED or ASSUMED.\n45\t\n46\t## 3. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n47\t\n48\t| Decision | Reversibility | Default (chosen now) | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n49\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n50\t| Consistency vs availability | R2/R3 + one-clause reason | … | … | V…, a cheap check, or the cited basis | … (for a gated row: \"V… fails, or …\") |\n51\t| Monolith vs services | … | … | … | … | … |\n52\t| Sync vs async | … | … | … | … | … |\n53\t| Build vs buy | … | … | … | … | … |\n54\t| Data-privacy boundary (personal or regulated data) | … | … | … | … | … |\n55\t| <each system-specific R2/R3 decision, e.g. the tenancy model> | … | … | … | … | … |\n56\t| (Brownfield) migration strategy, coexistence and cutover, rollback, system of record | … | … | … | … | … |\n57\t| (AI) prompt+RAG vs fine-tune | … | … | … | … | … |\n58\t| (AI) hosted API vs self-host | … | … | … | … | … |\n59\t\n60\t**R1 defaults:** <decision> → <default>; … (one line; no rows for R1 decisions).\n61\t**N/A:** <considered decisions that do not apply> — <reason> (one line).\n62\tOmit the (Brownfield) and (AI) rows when they do not apply. Inherited brownfield decisions the\n63\tplan will not change are listed once as constraints, not as rows.\n64\t\n65\t## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n66\t- The one real request and the real response.\n67\t- Every tier it crosses.\n68\t- How it is deployed, logged, monitored, and rolled back on day zero.\n69\t- Who can reach it (internal or allow-listed traffic behind a flag until its controls exist).\n70\t\n71\tIf an exception changes Phase 0, say so in one line and cite it (E…).\n72\tExit check (V0): a real request succeeds with one trace across every tier; a deploy and a\n73\trollback succeed through the pipeline; an injected failure fires an alert; the first values of\n74\tthe measurable budgets are recorded as baselines, not targets.\n75\t\n76\t## 5. Cross-cutting concerns (per phase, from the first commit)\n96\t\n97\t| Phase | Security | Observability | Reproducibility | Resilience |\n98\t|---|---|---|---|---|\n99\t| 0 | … | … | … | … |\n100\t\n101\tObservability appears in Phase 0. AI layer (AI/agentic systems only)\n105\t\n106\t| Sublayer | In this system | Built in | Exit check or V-ID |\n107\t|---|---|---|---|\n108\t| 1. Feedback | … | … | … |\n117\t\n118\tA capability sublayer (4–9) this system does not need: \"Not needed — <reason>\". {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01X1h3uygjFbGaqBLhvdpgoP","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Worked examples: dependencies, validation gates, labels, reversibility, budgets, exceptions\n2\t\n3\tExamples for the rules in `SKILL.md`. This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\n4\tsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n5\t\n6\t## 1. Dependency kinds\n7\t\n8\t| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n9\t|---|---|---|---|\n10\t| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n11\t| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n12\t| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n13\t| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n14\t| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n15\t| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n16\t| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n17\t\n18\tCommon misses:\n19\t\n20\t- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n21\t- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n22\t  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n23\t- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n24\t- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n25\t\n26\t## 2. Validation gates\n27\t\n28\tFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n29\t\n30\t| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n31\t|---|---|---|---|---|\n32\t| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n33\t| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n34\t| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n35\t| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n36\t| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n37\t\n38\tShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\n39\tso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n40\t\n41\tA good acceptance threshold:\n42\t\n43\t- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n44\t  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n45\t  security, or legal judgment;\n46\t- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n47\t- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n48\t- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n49\t\n50\tAnti-patterns:\n51\t\n52\t- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n53\t  correct, or affordable enough.\n54\t- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n55\t  UNKNOWN has no number.\n56\t- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n57\t  sublayer.\n58\t- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n59\t- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n60\t  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n61\t\n62\t## 3. Reversibility\n63\t\n64\t| Tier | Examples |\n65\t|---|---|\n66\t| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n67\t| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n68\t| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n69\t\n70\tCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\n71\tbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\n72\tundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\n73\tirreversible operation.\n74\t\n75\tBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\n76\tprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n77\t\n78\tSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\n79\tinterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\n80\traw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\n81\tthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\n82\ton every row from day one.\n83\t\n84\t## 4. Budgets\n85\t\n86\t| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n87\t|---|---|---|---|\n88\t| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n89\t| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n90\t| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n91\t| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n92\t| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n93\t\n94\tRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). Unknowns are fine; fabricated certainty\n95\tis not. The walking skeleton measures the first real values, and later gates check against them.\n96\t\n97\t## 5. Methodology exceptions\n98\t\n99\t| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n100\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n101\t| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; if it fails, re-scope or stop |\n102\t| E2 | Skeleton runs in production (principle 6) | Certified medical device: nothing reaches production before clearance | Skeleton runs in a production-equivalent environment on target hardware, under design controls | Verification records traceable into the submission | Permanent for the certified scope: every release passes change control, and a significant change needs re-submission unless an approved change-control plan covers it; uncertified back-office tools follow the normal order |\n103\t| E3 | Dependency order (principle 1) | A regulatory date fixes when the reporting feature ships, before its data source is validated | Build behind a flag against the source's contract, with contract tests, and keep an interim manual report that meets the date | Contract tests pass against the real source, and report totals reconcile with the system of record | The source's validation gate passes; the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n104\t| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n105\t\n106\tNot exceptions:\n107\t\n108\t- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n109\t- Brownfield work. Example of the normal method: a CI/CD platform for 50 services takes one real\n110\t  service through the new platform to production in Phase 0, with its old pipeline kept as the\n111\t  fallback, and migrates the rest in waves.\n112\t- Reading principle 6 for software you do not operate: a CLI's skeleton is the released package,\n113\t  installed the way users install it, renaming a real folder in dry-run mode (writes run on a\n114\t  disposable copy until the undo journal's gate passes).\n115\t- Data-protection regimes (HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR). This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\nsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n\n## 1. Dependency kinds\n\n| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n\nCommon misses:\n\n- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n\n## 2. Validation gates\n\nFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n\n| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n\nShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\nso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n\nA good acceptance threshold:\n\n- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n  security, or legal judgment;\n- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n\nAnti-patterns:\n\n- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n  correct, or affordable enough.\n- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n  UNKNOWN has no number.\n- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n  sublayer.\n- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n\n## 3. Reversibility\n\n| Tier | Examples |\n|---|---|\n| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n\nCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\nbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\nundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\nirreversible operation.\n\nBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\nprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n\nSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\ninterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\nraw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\nthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\non every row from day one.\n\n## 4. Budgets\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n\nRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n\nNot exceptions:\n\n- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n- Brownfield work. {"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-sonnet-5-5","id":"msg_bdrk_pf3wktingcvndv2duj7khbu4t27nmurj2ugk3p4qqsyvd5lov53a","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"# BUILD PLAN: Multi-tenant SaaS billing system\n\nThe request leaves scope open, so I made the assumptions below (see Missing inputs). Items marked ASSUMPTION are starting values to confirm. They are not requirements.\n\n## 1. Classification and constraints\n- **What:** A billing platform for a SaaS vendor's own customers (the tenants). It meters usage, rates it against plans, issues immutable invoices, collects payment through a processor, and keeps a double-entry ledger.\n- **Type:** Software, greenfield, **not small**. It handles money and personal data, and it is used by outside tenants.\n- **Dominant constraint:** Correctness, meaning money is exact and auditable and tenants are isolated.\n- **Worst failure:** Customers are charged the wrong amount (double, wrong, or unreversible), or usage is silently lost or duplicated, and nobody detects it. The second-worst failure is one tenant seeing another's billing data. V2 guards the first and V3 guards the second.\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Money accuracy | Zero ledger invariant violations; every invoice total equals an independent recalculation to the minor unit | ASSUMPTION: rounding and proration rules are to be signed off by Finance | V2, V6 |\n| Usage-ingest latency | p95 < 200 ms at projected peak | ASSUMPTION: a typical metering-API target | V0 baseline, V4 |\n| Throughput (usage events/s) | — | UNKNOWN: needs projected events per second at 12 months, from the product owner and finance, in Phase 0 | V4 |\n| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to, from the product owner, before Phase 5. Ledger writes favor correctness over uptime (see §3). | SLIs and burn-rate alerts in Phase 5 |\n| RPO / RTO | Ledger RPO ≤ 5 min, RTO ≤ 1 h | ASSUMPTION: managed Postgres multi-AZ with PITR; Finance to confirm | Restore drill in Phase 4 |\n| Bill-run duration | — | UNKNOWN: needs tenant count and invoice volume, from the product owner, before Phase 3 hardens | Phase 3 load test |\n| Operational complexity | One modular monolith, one worker, one managed Postgres; no self-run cluster | ASSUMPTION: a small team | Phase 5 exit check |\n\n**Missing inputs** (none changes the phase order unless noted):\n1. **Who the tenants are.** I assumed the vendor bills its own customers. If the platform bills on behalf of tenants (marketplace or Connect-style), the order changes. That case adds money-transmission, KYC, and payout dependencies before any live money. Confirm this first.\n2. The pricing models and the list of plans to support. V1 needs them.\n3. Currencies, tax jurisdictions and registrations, and legal invoice-numbering rules. They shape the R3 ledger schema, so they are needed before Phase 1 specifies it. The ledger is multi-currency-ready, with one currency enabled.\n4. Projected volume and the availability commitment (both UNKNOWN above).\n5. Cloud and stack. I assumed AWS.\n\n## 2. Dependency map\n\n| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Ledger schema and identifiers | Currencies, jurisdictions, and invoice-numbering rules (input 3) | decision / organizational | specified (Phase 1) |\n| Rating, proration, and invoicing | V2, plus Finance sign-off on rounding, proration, and credit rules | validation / decision | specified (Phase 3) |\n| Any non-internal tenant | V3 | risk-security | exposed |\n| Live card charging | V5 (SAQ A confirmed by the processor or a QSA), the processor's live-mode approval, and a DPA with the processor | risk-security / organizational | exposed |\n| Live tax calculation | Tax registrations and a tax-provider contract | organizational | deployed in live mode |\n| Bill-run and ingest sizing | Volume (UNKNOWN) and V4 | validation | hardened |\n| First real invoice and charge | V6, with a named Finance approver | risk-security / organizational | exposed |\n| Phase 1 design | V1 (build versus buy) | decision / validation | specified |\n\nOrganizational items start in Phase 0 because they have lead time: the processor account, the tax provider, the named Finance and security reviewers, and the DPAs.\n\nNo economic dependency binds beyond the cost comparison inside V1. No structural or runtime dependency is surprising.\n\n## 3. Tradeoff gates\n\n| Decision | Reversibility | Default | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Tenancy and isolation | R3: tenant data in a shared store can't be re-split cheaply, and a leak can't be undone | Shared Postgres schema. `tenant_id NOT NULL` leads every key and is on every row. Row-level security fails closed. A tenant-routing layer exists from Phase 1 as a seam. | No tenant needs physical isolation or residency. | V3 | V3 fails, or a contract requires dedicated storage or residency. In that case the affected tenant moves to its own database through the routing seam. |\n| Ledger model and identifiers | R3: real financial data and audit obligations | Append-only double-entry ledger. Money is integer minor units plus an ISO currency code. IDs are UUIDv7. Corrections are reversing entries, never updates. Finalized invoices are immutable, and credit notes correct them. | The pricing models fit entries plus rating rules. | V2 | V2 fails, or V1 shows a bought engine must be the system of record. |\n| Consistency vs availability | R3: it defines the money semantics | Ledger, invoice, and payment state are strongly consistent on a single-region multi-AZ primary, and ledger writes fail rather than diverge. Usage ingest is idempotent (unique on `tenant_id`+`event_key`) so clients can retry safely. | Brief write downtime costs less than a wrong charge. | V2, V4 | The SLO (once supplied) can't be met with one primary. Then add replicas for reads and degraded modes, but never relax ledger writes. |\n| Build vs buy: billing engine | R3: invoice history and customer-visible numbering migrate painfully | Build the ledger, rating, and invoicing. Buy payments, tax calculation, and email. | Planned pricing (usage tiers, custom contracts, credits) exceeds what Stripe Billing or Lago express cleanly. | V1 | V1 shows all planned plans fit a bought engine at lower total cost. In that case Phase 1 is replanned around an integration plus the ledger. |\n| Payment processor | R3: card tokens have gravity at the vendor | Stripe (or Adyen) behind a `PaymentProvider` interface. Card entry uses the hosted fields only. | The processor contract allows token export to another PCI-compliant processor. | V5, plus a contract clause check in Phase 0 | V5 fails, or the token-export clause is refused. Then choose another processor before Phase 4. |\n| Data-privacy boundary | R3: exposed personal data can't be recalled | Card data never touches our systems. Personal data (names, emails, addresses, tax IDs) lives in separate tables, with tax IDs encrypted at column level. The ledger holds only opaque IDs, so erasure doesn't break immutability. Logs and telemetry carry IDs only. | GDPR-style erasure and access requests will apply. | V5 (PAN scan), V3 (telemetry scan) | Legal review requires a regional data split. In that case, treat it as the tenancy flip. |\n| Monolith vs services | R2: internal boundaries | Modular monolith plus one worker process | One team | CI module-boundary lint, pass = 0 cross-module table accesses | V4 shows ingest needs independent scaling. Extract ingest. |\n| Sync vs async | R2 | Usage is written synchronously to a partitioned Postgres table. Aggregation and bill runs are async jobs with idempotent job keys. Payment state is webhook-driven, with webhooks deduplicated by event ID. | Postgres sustains ingest at 2× peak. | V4 | V4 fails. Add a durable log (Kafka/Kinesis) and an analytical store for usage. |\n\n**R1 defaults:** language → TypeScript (NestJS); cloud → AWS (ECS Fargate, RDS Postgres); IaC → Terraform; CI/CD → GitHub Actions; identity → managed OIDC provider (Cognito/Auth0); telemetry → OpenTelemetry to a managed backend; invoice PDF → server-side renderer.\n**N/A:** brownfield migration, since there is no existing billing system (confirm in Missing inputs); AI decisions, since there is no AI component.\n\n## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n- **The one real request:** An internal \"house\" tenant authenticates through OIDC and sends `POST /v1/usage-events` with an idempotency key. Rows are written under row-level security. A worker aggregates the usage and builds a draft invoice for a one-line flat-plus-usage plan. Ledger entries are posted. The invoice is finalized and a payment is created at the processor **in test mode** with a test token. The webhook returns, a payment entry is posted, and `GET /v1/invoices/{id}` shows the invoice as paid.\n- **Tiers crossed:** Edge/WAF → API → auth → Postgres with RLS → worker → processor sandbox → webhook → API.\n- **Deploy:** Terraform and GitHub Actions deploy to the production account, with blue/green on Fargate. Migrations are expand/contract, and the feature flag defaults to off.\n- **Logged and monitored:** Structured JSON logs with `trace_id` and `tenant_id`, and no personal data or card data. One OpenTelemetry trace spans every tier. Alarms cover API errors, worker failures, webhook lag, and ledger imbalance. Telemetry that records amounts is classed confidential.\n- **Rolled back:** The deploy is rolled back once through the pipeline, including an expand/contract migration step.\n- **Who can reach it:** Allow-listed IPs plus an internal OIDC group, behind the flag. No real tenant, and no live-mode processor keys or real money. The payment tier is a disposable sandbox.\n- **Also started in Phase 0:** The organizational items in §2. The V1 fit-gap starts here and must finish before Phase 1 specifies the ledger. Volume and currency inputs are collected.\n\n**Exit check (V0):** The request succeeds with one trace across every tier. A deploy and a rollback succeed through the pipeline. An injected failure (worker killed, webhook dropped) fires an alert. Baselines are recorded: ingest p95 at near-zero load, and the time from usage to paid invoice.\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n- **Phase 1: Tenancy, identity, ledger, API contract** (widest blast radius first)\n  - Unlocks: Everything else. Schema and API shape are the costliest things to change.\n  - Depends on: Phase 0, V1 and V0, and currency and jurisdiction inputs.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Tenant model and routing seam, with row-level security as the default on every table.\n    2. Auth: service and user principals, and per-tenant scopes.\n    3. Ledger schema and posting API (double-entry, idempotent posting).\n    4. Versioned OpenAPI contract with idempotency keys and error semantics.\n    5. Audit log.\n    6. Run the V2 property tests in CI from the first ledger commit, and the V3 cross-tenant suite in CI from the first endpoint.\n  - Rollback: Expand/contract migrations and flag off. No tenant data exists yet.\n  - Exit check: V2 and the first pass of V3 run green in CI. CI fails on any table without RLS and `tenant_id`.\n\n- **Phase 2: Metering**\n  - Unlocks: Rating on trusted usage.\n  - Depends on: Phase 1, and the volume input (UNKNOWN, due in Phase 0).\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Idempotent ingest API with late and out-of-order handling.\n    2. Partitioned usage store.\n    3. Aggregation jobs.\n    4. Replay tool.\n    5. Load test (V4).\n  - Rollback: Flag off. Usage is replayable from raw events, and the raw events are retained.\n  - Exit check: V4 passes.\n\n- **Phase 3: Catalog, rating, subscriptions, invoicing**\n  - Unlocks: Correct invoices in shadow.\n  - Depends on: V2, V4, and Finance sign-off on rules.\n  - Tasks:\n    1. Plan catalog (flat, per-seat, tiered, usage).\n    2. Rating engine as pure functions, golden-tested.\n    3. Subscription lifecycle: upgrade, downgrade, proration, cancel.\n    4. Invoice generation, finalization, and credit notes.\n    5. Tax-provider integration in test mode.\n    6. Bill-run sizing.\n  - Rollback: Invoices stay draft until V6. Drafts can be voided and regenerated.\n  - Exit check: Golden scenarios (as many as the plan list requires) reproduce the independent recalculation. The bill-run load test meets a Finance-approved duration once the UNKNOWN is resolved.\n\n- **Phase 4: Payments, dunning, reconciliation**\n  - Unlocks: Readiness for live money.\n  - Depends on: Phase 3, and V5 (started in Phase 0).\n  - Tasks:\n    1. `PaymentProvider` adapter (hosted fields, webhooks, refunds).\n    2. Dunning and retry schedule.\n    3. Daily reconciliation of the ledger against processor reports.\n    4. Backup restore drill against RPO and RTO.\n    5. PAN scan of logs and databases.\n  - Rollback: Processor stays in test mode. Live keys are not provisioned until V5 passes.\n  - Exit check: V5 passes. Reconciliation runs with zero unexplained differences on test data. The restore drill meets the RPO and RTO ASSUMPTION.\n\n- **Phase 5: Controlled exposure**\n  - Unlocks: General availability.\n  - Depends on: V2, V3, V5, V6, and the availability SLO input.\n  - Tasks, smallest exposure first:\n    1. Shadow bill run: compute invoices for internal tenants and pilot tenants, with no charges and no customer emails.\n    2. V6 go/no-go.\n    3. One pilot tenant goes live, then about 10, then all, each widening only after the previous step's reconciliation is clean.\n    4. SLIs and burn-rate alerts against the SLO.\n  - Rollback: Per-tenant flag back to shadow. Refund and credit-note procedure for charges made.\n  - **Point of no return:** The first customer-visible invoice and real charge. It is guarded by V6.\n  - Exit check: V6 passes, and at least one full live cycle reconciles clean per widening step.\n\n## 6. Validation gates\n\n| ID | Hypothesis | Method | Acceptance threshold | Evidence | Unlocks (and if it fails) | Phase |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| V0 | A change can be deployed, observed, and rolled back through every tier in production | Skeleton run | The V0 exit check in §4 | Pipeline run logs and the trace export, kept with the release | Phase 1 | 0 |\n| V1 | The planned pricing cannot be met by a bought engine at comparable total cost | Fit-gap of the planned plans against Stripe Billing and Lago, with a 3-year cost comparison | Named sign-off by the product owner and Finance on build versus buy. The plan list is UNKNOWN until supplied, so it is needed in Phase 0. | Fit-gap matrix and cost sheet in the repo | Phase 1 build-path; if it fails, replan around the bought engine | Starts and ends in 0 |\n| V2 | The ledger cannot lose, duplicate, or misstate money under retries, concurrency, and replays | Property-based tests over randomized postings with duplicate requests, concurrent posts, and replayed webhooks. These are design parameters, not measured baselines. | Test reports stored in CI artifacts | Phase 3 spec and any live money; if it fails, fix the model, and the R3 schema is reopened | Starts in 1, required before 3 |\n| V3 | A tenant cannot read or write another tenant's data by any path | Cross-tenant automated suite over every endpoint, job, cache, and export. Then a scan of logs and telemetry for other tenants' identifiers. Then an independent penetration test on the isolation paths. | 0 cross-tenant reads or writes across the suite. A named security reviewer's pass/fail sign-off. | Suite report and the reviewer's sign-off in the security folder | Any non-internal tenant; if it fails, fix and re-test, and the dedicated-storage flip is considered | Starts in 1, required before 5 |\n| V4 | Postgres ingest sustains 2× projected peak with duplicates and late events, and replay reproduces identical totals | Load test at 2× peak on 12-month-sized data, long enough to span autovacuum and checkpoints. Then replay from raw events. | Zero lost events, aggregates identical after replay, and p95 < 200 ms (ASSUMPTION). The peak itself is UNKNOWN, so it is a prerequisite input. | Benchmark report stored with the build | Phase 3 sizing; if it fails, add the durable log and analytical store (§3) | 2 |\n| V5 | Hosted card entry keeps us at SAQ A and no card number exists in our systems | Data-flow review by the processor or a QSA. Then a PAN scan of logs, databases, and backups. | Written confirmation of SAQ A eligibility and a PAN scan that finds none | Completed SAQ A and scan report | Live-mode keys and live charging; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | Starts in 0, required before 5 |\n| V6 | The first real invoices are correct, and we can reverse a mistake | Shadow bill run for a full cycle over internal and pilot tenants, compared against an independent recalculation by Finance. Rehearse refund and credit-note reversal. | 100% of invoices match to the minor unit (ASSUMPTION; rounding rules from Finance). The named Finance approver signs the go/no-go. | Shadow-run comparison report with counts and IDs only (no customer records) | Pilot, then widening; if it fails, stay in shadow and fix | 5 |\n\n## 7. Cross-cutting concerns\n\n| Phase | Security | Observability | Reproducibility | Resilience |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 0 | OIDC, allow-list, flag off, sandbox-only payments, secrets in a manager, no personal data or card data in logs | Trace, logs, alarms, V0 baselines, telemetry classed confidential | Terraform, pinned images, one-command deploy | Rollback drill, expand/contract migrations |\n| 1 | RLS fail-closed, CI guard on tenant columns, scoped API credentials, immutable audit log | Per-tenant metrics, ledger-imbalance alarm | Migrations in CI, schema snapshots | Idempotent posting, PITR enabled |\n| 2 | Ingest authentication and per-tenant rate limits | Ingest lag, duplicate, and late-event counters | Raw events retained, replay tool | Retry-safe ingest, backlog alarms |\n| 3 | Finalized invoices immutable, plus approval for manual adjustments | Rating traces, bill-run progress, failure counts | Golden fixtures, versioned pricing rules | Idempotent job keys, resumable bill runs |\n| 4 | Hosted fields only, webhook signature checks, PAN scan, key rotation | Webhook lag, reconciliation differences | Processor contract tests, pinned API version | Webhook dedupe and replay, restore drill |\n| 5 | V3 and V5 verified before exposure, least-privilege operators, access logs | SLIs, burn-rate alerts, on-call runbooks | Release tagged per tenant wave | Per-tenant flag back to shadow, refund and credit-note runbook |\n\n## 8. AI layer\nN/A — no AI component.\n\n## 9. Methodology exceptions\nNone.\n\n## 10. Deliberately deferred\n- Dedicated per-tenant databases. Pulled forward by a contract requiring isolation or residency (the §3 tenancy flip).\n- Durable log and analytical store for usage. Pulled forward if V4 fails.\n- Extracting services from the monolith. Pulled forward if V4 or ownership boundaries demand independent scaling.\n- Multi-currency enablement and FX. The schema is ready. Pulled forward when the first non-base-currency tenant signs.\n- Revenue recognition and tax filing. Pulled forward when Finance needs them before the first audit.\n- Customer self-serve portal beyond hosted invoices. Pulled forward when support volume justifies it.\n- Billing on behalf of tenants (marketplace payouts). Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n- **The one real request:** An internal \"house\" tenant authenticates through OIDC and sends `POST /v1/usage-events` with an idempotency key. Rows are written under row-level security. A worker aggregates the usage and builds a draft invoice for a one-line flat-plus-usage plan. Ledger entries are posted. The invoice is finalized and a payment is created at the processor **in test mode** with a test token. The webhook returns, a payment entry is posted, and `GET /v1/invoices/{id}` shows the invoice as paid.\n- **Tiers crossed:** Edge/WAF → API → auth → Postgres with RLS → worker → processor sandbox → webhook → API.\n- **Deploy:** Terraform and GitHub Actions deploy to the production account, with blue/green on Fargate. Migrations are expand/contract, and the feature flag defaults to off.\n- **Logged and monitored:** Structured JSON logs with `trace_id` and `tenant_id`, and no personal data or card data. One OpenTelemetry trace spans every tier. Alarms cover API errors, worker failures, webhook lag, and ledger imbalance. Telemetry that records amounts is classed confidential.\n- **Rolled back:** The deploy is rolled back once through the pipeline, including an expand/contract migration step.\n- **Who can reach it:** Allow-listed IPs plus an internal OIDC group, behind the flag. No real tenant, and no live-mode processor keys or real money. The payment tier is a disposable sandbox.\n- **Also started in Phase 0:** The organizational items in §2. The V1 fit-gap starts here and must finish before Phase 1 specifies the ledger. Volume and currency inputs are collected.\n\n**Exit check (V0):** The request succeeds with one trace across every tier. A deploy and a rollback succeed through the pipeline. An injected failure (worker killed, webhook dropped) fires an alert. Baselines are recorded: ingest p95 at near-zero load, and the time from usage to paid invoice.\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n- **Phase 1: Tenancy, identity, ledger, API contract** (widest blast radius first)\n  - Unlocks: Everything else. Tenant model and routing seam, with row-level security as the default on every table.\n    2. Auth: service and user principals, and per-tenant scopes.\n    3. Ledger schema and posting API (double-entry, idempotent posting).\n    4. Versioned OpenAPI contract with idempotency keys and error semantics.\n    5. Audit log.\n    6. Run the V2 property tests in CI from the first ledger commit, and the V3 cross-tenant suite in CI from the first endpoint.\n  - Rollback: Expand/contract migrations and flag off. No tenant data exists yet.\n  - Exit check: V2 and the first pass of V3 run green in CI. PAN scan of logs and databases.\n  - Rollback: Processor stays in test mode. Live keys are not provisioned until V5 passes.\n  - Exit check: V5 passes. Reconciliation runs with zero unexplained differences on test data. The restore drill meets the RPO and RTO ASSUMPTION.\n\n- **Phase 5: Controlled exposure**\n  - Unlocks: General availability.\n  - Depends on: V2, V3, V5, V6, and the availability SLO input.\n  - Tasks, smallest exposure first:\n    1. Shadow bill run: compute invoices for internal tenants and pilot tenants, with no charges and no customer emails.\n    2. V6 go/no-go.\n    3. One pilot tenant goes live, then about 10, then all, each widening only after the previous step's reconciliation is clean.\n    4. SLIs and burn-rate alerts against the SLO.\n  - Rollback: Per-tenant flag back to shadow. Refund and credit-note procedure for charges made.\n  - **Point of no return:** The first customer-visible invoice and real charge. It is guarded by V6.\n  - Exit check: V6 passes, and at least one full live cycle reconciles clean per widening step.\n\n## 6.
